title: How We Know
theme: Science: theory, evidence and the limits of certainty
objectives: I can explain how a scientific theory differs from an everyday guess.
I can tell quantitative evidence from qualitative evidence and say when each is useful.
I can spot a confounding variable and an anomaly in a description of an experiment.
I can write a short evaluation of an investigation using at least four words from this unit.
rationale: Eighth-grade science asks students to judge investigations, not just carry them out. The unit gives three exact terms for explaining (theory, paradigm, causation) and the words for designing and judging evidence (empirical, replicate, quantitative, qualitative, confound, rigorous, anomaly). Theory is taught with its everyday sense beside its scientific one, because that mismatch causes many misconceptions. The words extend the statistics vocabulary of grade 7 and prepare students to read lab reports, news about studies, and the arguments in later units about technology and consequences.

words.def: In science, a well-tested explanation of how something works, supported by many kinds of evidence.

senses.def: In everyday talk, a guess or personal idea that has not been tested.
senses.example: My theory is that the cat hides because she hates the vacuum cleaner.

words.ex: The theory of plate tectonics explains why earthquakes and volcanoes cluster along certain boundaries.
words.ex2: Germ theory changed medicine by showing that many diseases are caused by tiny living organisms.
words.nonExample: A hunch that nobody has tested is not yet a scientific theory.

apps.academic: A scientific theory is stronger than a hypothesis because it has survived many different tests.
apps.spoken: Scientists call it a theory because it explains many observations, not because it is a guess.
apps.writing: Avoid writing just a theory about a scientific theory; name the evidence that supports it instead.

cloze.s: Unlike a quick guess, a scientific ___ about how continents move is supported by evidence from geology, fossils, and satellites.

cloze2.s: Biologists rely on the cell ___, which holds that all living things are made of cells.

misuse.s: A scientific theory is a wild guess that nobody has ever tested or checked against evidence.
misuse.why: In science a theory is well tested and widely supported; an untested wild guess is closer to a hunch.

visual.alt: A telescope beside a stack of science books.

words.frame: A scientific theory is stronger than a guess because ___.

words.def: A shared set of ideas and methods that people in a field use to understand their subject.
words.ex: For centuries an Earth-centered paradigm guided astronomers, until evidence for a Sun-centered model piled up.
words.ex2: The invention of the microscope helped move biology toward a new paradigm built around cells.
words.nonExample: A single experiment is not a paradigm, because a paradigm is a framework many researchers share.
words.rel: the framework a field works inside

apps.academic: Historians of science use the phrase paradigm shift for a time when a field changes its basic assumptions.
apps.spoken: Smartphones changed the paradigm for how we take and share photos.
apps.writing: Use paradigm for a whole framework of ideas and methods, not for a single idea or a single tool.

cloze.s: For hundreds of years the Earth-centered ___ shaped how astronomers explained the motion of the planets.

cloze2.s: When enough strange results pile up, a field may have to give up its old ___ and adopt a new one.

misuse.s: A paradigm is one measurement of a plant's height written in a single student's notebook.
misuse.why: A paradigm is a shared framework of ideas and methods, not one measurement in one notebook.

visual.alt: A web of connected ideas and methods that together make up a shared framework.

words.def: A relationship in which one event or condition makes another one happen.
words.ex: Doctors needed many careful studies to establish the causation between smoking and lung disease.
words.ex2: Two graphs that rise together do not prove causation, because a third factor may be driving both.
words.nonExample: Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise in summer, but that is correlation, not causation.

morph.note: The final e of cause is dropped before -ation.

apps.academic: Controlled experiments test causation by changing one variable while holding the others steady.
apps.spoken: Just because two things happened together does not prove causation.
apps.writing: Write is associated with for a pattern, and save causes for a result that supports causation.

cloze.s: The scientists could not claim ___ until a controlled experiment showed that changing the diet changed the outcome.

cloze2.s: Because the study showed only that two things happened together, the editor warned writers not to imply ___.

misuse.s: Because the rooster crows before sunrise, causation proves that the rooster makes the sun rise.
misuse.why: Happening first does not prove cause; the rooster and the sunrise are linked by time, not by causation.

visual.alt: An arrow leading from a box labeled cause to a box labeled effect.

words.frame: To show causation, a researcher would need ___.

words.def: Based on observation, measurement, or experiment rather than on opinion or idea alone.
words.ex: The astronomer wanted empirical evidence, not just a clever idea, before announcing the discovery.
words.ex2: Her claim about sleep and memory rests on empirical data from two hundred students.
words.nonExample: An argument about how things ought to be, with no measurements, is not empirical.

apps.academic: Empirical studies collect measurements, while theoretical work builds models to explain them.
apps.spoken: Do you have any empirical evidence, or is that just a feeling?
apps.writing: Put empirical before evidence, data, or study to show that it was observed or measured.

cloze.s: The committee rejected the proposal because it offered no ___ evidence, only opinions about what should happen.

cloze2.s: Her ___ study counted and measured every bird that visited the feeder over six months.

misuse.s: The researchers' conclusion was entirely empirical because they never made a single observation or measurement.
misuse.why: Empirical means based on observation and measurement; a conclusion with none is the opposite.

visual.alt: A microscope next to a ruler.

words.frame: Empirical evidence for this claim would be ___.

words.def: To repeat an experiment or study to see whether the same result happens again.
words.ex: Other labs tried to replicate the surprising result, but their measurements did not match.
words.ex2: Because the team wrote down every step, a school in another state could replicate the experiment.
words.nonExample: Reading about an experiment in a magazine is not the same as replicating it.

apps.academic: A finding becomes widely trusted when independent researchers replicate it.
apps.spoken: Can you replicate that trick, or was it just luck?
apps.writing: In a lab report, describe your steps so clearly that another person could replicate them.

cloze.s: To check the surprising result, the team asked another laboratory to ___ the experiment using the same materials and steps.

cloze2.s: Nobody could ___ the startling discovery, so scientists began to suspect a mistake in the first test.

misuse.s: The students replicated the experiment by changing every step, every material, and the question being asked.
misuse.why: To replicate is to repeat; changing everything makes it a different experiment.

visual.alt: A test tube beside a circular arrow.

words.frame: A result is more believable if others can replicate it because ___.

words.def: Something that does not fit the usual pattern or what was expected.
words.ex: The wilted plant was an anomaly in a row of healthy, thriving seedlings.
words.ex2: Astronomers studied an anomaly in the orbit of Uranus and eventually predicted the existence of Neptune.
words.nonExample: A reading that matches the other thirty readings is not an anomaly.
words.rel: the thing that does not fit

apps.academic: In data analysis, an anomaly may be an error, or it may be the clue to something new.
apps.spoken: That one warm day in January was an anomaly.
apps.writing: Do not delete an anomaly; explain it, or say honestly that you cannot yet.

cloze.s: In a table of steady temperatures, the sudden spike at noon looked like an ___, so the scientists checked the thermometer.

cloze2.s: One cool afternoon was an ___ in a heat wave that otherwise lasted two weeks.

misuse.s: The scientist called the result an anomaly because it matched every one of the other measurements exactly.
misuse.why: An anomaly is something that does not fit the pattern; a result that matches every other one fits it perfectly.

visual.alt: A single red dot among a crowd of blue dots.

words.frame: An anomaly in my data might mean ___.

words.def: Based on numbers or amounts that can be measured and counted.
words.ex: Quantitative data, such as heights in centimeters, let the club compare plants with exact numbers.
words.ex2: A quantitative survey counted how many students walked, biked, or rode the bus to school.
words.nonExample: A description of a painting's mood is not quantitative data.

apps.academic: Quantitative evidence answers questions that begin with how many or how much.
apps.spoken: I need quantitative proof, like actual numbers, before I change the plan.
apps.writing: Pair quantitative data with units so readers know what the numbers measure.

cloze.s: The ___ part of the report listed the exact height, mass, and temperature of every sample.

cloze2.s: To make the survey ___, the class counted how many students chose each option instead of collecting comments.

misuse.s: Her quantitative notes described the mood of the room without a single number or measurement.
misuse.why: Quantitative data are numbers or measurements; a description of a mood has neither.

visual.alt: A bar chart beside a row of numbers.

words.def: Based on descriptions of features such as color, texture, or opinion, rather than on numbers.
words.ex: The botanist's qualitative notes described the leaves as glossy, dark green, and slightly curled.
words.ex2: Qualitative interviews captured how students felt about the new schedule in their own words.
words.nonExample: A table of exact measurements in millimeters is quantitative, not qualitative.

apps.academic: Qualitative evidence helps explain why a pattern appears, not just how large it is.
apps.spoken: I have no numbers, only qualitative observations about what I saw.
apps.writing: Make qualitative details specific, such as glossy and curled, rather than vague words like nice.

cloze.s: Besides measuring height, the club kept ___ notes about each leaf's color, shape, and texture.

cloze2.s: The researcher's ___ study collected stories, quotations, and descriptions rather than counting responses.

misuse.s: The qualitative data in the table were exact measurements in grams, written to two decimal places.
misuse.why: Qualitative data describe qualities; exact measurements in grams are quantitative.

visual.alt: A paintbrush beside a notebook of written observations.

words.frame: A qualitative observation of ___ would be ___.

words.def: To mix an unplanned factor into a test so that you cannot tell what caused the result.

senses.def: To confuse or puzzle someone completely.
senses.example: The magician's trick confounded the entire audience.

words.ex: A second variable, such as sunlight, can confound an experiment about fertilizer.
words.ex2: Testing on different days might confound the comparison if the weather changes.
words.nonExample: Changing only one thing at a time keeps an experiment from being confounded.

apps.academic: A confounding variable changes along with the factor being tested, which makes the results unclear.
apps.spoken: If we test on different days, the weather could confound our results.
apps.writing: Name the confounding variable, then explain how you would control it.

cloze.s: If one group of plants gets more light than the other, the extra light will ___ the comparison of fertilizers.

cloze2.s: Testing new shoes on elite sprinters and old shoes on beginners would ___ the results, because skill would be mixed in with shoe quality.

misuse.s: To confound the experiment, the scientist made sure that only one variable changed so the results were perfectly clear.
misuse.why: To confound is to mix in an extra factor; changing only one variable is how to avoid that.

visual.alt: Tangled arrows leading into a test tube.

words.frame: A hidden variable can confound a test when ___.

words.def: Extremely careful, thorough, and exact, with no room for sloppy mistakes.
words.ex: The lab's rigorous testing included three independent trials and a check of every instrument.
words.ex2: Our history teacher is rigorous about citing sources, and she marks every unsupported claim.
words.nonExample: Guessing the answer and skipping the check is not rigorous work.

apps.academic: A rigorous experiment controls variables, uses enough samples, and records every step.
apps.spoken: Her training schedule is rigorous: she practices before school and after.
apps.writing: Rigorous praises method, not mood, so say what made the work rigorous.

cloze.s: The ___ inspection checked every weld on the bridge twice, using two different instruments.

cloze2.s: Because the scientists were so ___ about recording every step, other teams could repeat the work exactly.

misuse.s: The lab's rigorous approach was to skip the measurements and trust whatever felt right.
misuse.why: Rigorous means exact and thorough; skipping measurements is sloppy, the opposite.

visual.alt: A drafting triangle next to a checklist with check marks.

passage.title: Why the Beans Disagreed
paras: Ms. Okoye's science club tested a new liquid fertilizer on bean plants. For two weeks the members measured each plant's height in centimeters, which gave them quantitative data, and they also described leaf color and shape, which gave them qualitative notes. The fertilized plants grew taller. “That proves it,” said Dev.

“One trial proves very little,” said Ms. Okoye. “Scientists trust a result only when others can replicate it. Does anything about your setup seem likely to confound the results?” Mina frowned at the photographs. The fertilized plants had sat on the sunny windowsill, while the others stood in a dim corner. Light, not fertilizer, might explain the difference.

The club designed a more rigorous test. They gave forty plants identical soil and light, assigned each plant to a group by drawing names from a hat, and recorded every measurement in a shared table. This empirical evidence, gathered by observation rather than argument, would let them check their claim fairly.

In the second trial one fertilized plant wilted, an anomaly that did not fit the pattern. Dev wanted to delete it. Ms. Okoye shook her head. “Anomalies can be the most interesting data you have,” she said, and she told them about the 1840s, when astronomers noticed that Uranus did not follow its predicted orbit. Instead of ignoring the problem, they proposed that an unseen planet was pulling on it, and in 1846 Neptune was found where the calculations pointed. The club checked the wilted plant and found mold in its pot.

At the end, the fertilized plants averaged about twenty percent taller. Mina wrote that the fertilizer was the cause, but Ms. Okoye asked her to be careful: causation is hard to establish, and this test showed it only for beans, in this soil, under this light. She added that people use theory casually to mean a guess, whereas in science a theory is a well-tested explanation supported by many kinds of evidence. Over time, anomalies can pile up until a whole paradigm, the shared set of assumptions scientists work within, gives way to a new one, as when astronomers accepted that Earth orbits the Sun.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word “confound” most nearly means
choices: prove beyond any doubt
repeat a trial exactly
record in a table
mix in an extra factor that hides the true cause
qs.why: Ms. Okoye asks what might confound the results, and Mina finds that sunlight, not fertilizer, might explain the difference.

qs.q: Why does Ms. Okoye refuse to let Dev delete the wilted plant?
choices: An anomaly may point to a problem or a discovery worth investigating.
She wants a perfect row of plants for the photographs.
She believes one plant can never matter to the results.
The school rules forbid removing any plant from a test.
qs.why: She says anomalies can be the most interesting data, and the story of Uranus shows how an odd result led to a discovery. The club also checks the plant and finds mold.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that the second trial was more rigorous than the first?
choices: The plants were measured in centimeters.
Mina wrote the conclusion for the club.
The plants shared identical soil and light and were assigned to groups by drawing names.
The fertilized plants grew taller than the others.
qs.why: Controlling soil and light and choosing groups by chance removed the problem that confounded the first trial.

qs.q: Why does Ms. Okoye ask Mina to be careful about saying the fertilizer was “the cause”?
choices: Fertilizer can never make plants grow taller.
The test showed causation only for these beans, in this soil, under this light.
Mina had measured the plants with the wrong tool.
A scientific theory cannot involve cause and effect.
qs.why: She points out that causation is hard to establish and that the test supports the claim only under the conditions of the experiment.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Fertilizer always makes bean plants grow taller.
Scientists should delete any measurement that looks strange.
A single experiment is enough to prove a theory.
Trustworthy science relies on careful design, repeated tests, and honest treatment of surprising data.
qs.why: The club learns to replicate, control for confounding factors, keep anomalies, and limit claims about causation.

write.prompt: Think of an investigation you have done or read about, such as a science fair project or a news story about a study. Use at least three words from this unit to say what made it strong or weak.
write.frame: The investigation was ___ because ___, but it could be improved by ___.

study.task: Choose three words from the unit that end in -ation, -ous, or -ical. For each, write the base word or noun it comes from, say what the ending adds, and use the word in a sentence about an experiment. Then explain the difference between quantity and quality and how it shows up in quantitative and qualitative.

words for gathering and checking evidence
problems that can arise in an investigation

shades.label: how well supported an explanation is

choices: rigorous : sloppy
theory : guess
qualitative : descriptions
anomaly : table
analogies.relation: the type of evidence and what it is made of

choices: thorough : careless
experiment : laboratory
hammer : nail

sentences: Write a sentence that uses theory in its scientific sense and names the evidence behind it.
Write a sentence about a test that would be confounded and name the extra factor.
Write a sentence that uses both quantitative and qualitative to describe how you would study a plant's growth.
Write a sentence about an anomaly in a set of results and say what a careful scientist should do about it.

given: The first test used a sunny window.
The second test used the same light for every plant.
combine.model: Because the second test gave every plant the same light, it was a more rigorous test than the first, which used a sunny window.

given: Neither lab got the same result.
combine.model: Because neither lab could replicate the result of the experiment, scientists began to doubt the discovery.

discuss: Why do people say just a theory, and why does that phrase mislead in science?
When might qualitative evidence be more useful than quantitative evidence? Use both words.
How can a scientist tell whether an anomaly is a mistake or a clue?
produce.explain: Explain the difference between correlation and causation using the word causation and an example from everyday life.

argue.prompt: Claim: A news story about a single study should not be believed until other researchers replicate its results. Take a side and support it with two reasons using words from this unit.
argue.frame: I believe that ___ because ___. A rigorous reader would ___, but a single study can still ___.

constructed.prompt: A student wants to test whether music helps classmates remember words, but one group studies in the morning and the other at night. Explain how that confounds the test and how to make it more rigorous.
look: names time of day as the extra factor
constructed.model: The time of day could confound the results, because people may remember better in the morning. A more rigorous test would have both groups study at the same time and change only the music.

constructed.prompt: You are studying how a new school lunch menu is working. Describe one quantitative and one qualitative way to gather evidence, and say what each would show.
look: gives a numerical method such as counting trays or waste
gives a descriptive method such as interviews or notes and says what it adds
constructed.model: A quantitative method is to weigh the food thrown away each day, which shows how much is left uneaten. A qualitative method is to interview students about taste and portion size, which shows why they eat or skip a meal.

constructed.prompt: One result in your experiment does not fit the pattern. Explain what you would do about the anomaly and how replicating the experiment could help.
look: explains that repeating the test shows whether the result happens again
constructed.model: I would keep the anomaly in my notes and try to explain it. Then I would replicate the experiment. If the odd result appears again, it may be a real clue, and if it never returns, it was probably an error.

teacher.overview: Students use ten words to describe, design, and judge investigations. They contrast the scientific and everyday meanings of theory, separate quantitative from qualitative evidence, practice spotting confounding variables and anomalies, and read a narrative in which a science club improves its experiment. The unit extends grade 7's work on hypotheses and statistics and prepares for later units on technology and consequences.

notes.va.theory.n: Theory is the unit's key multiple-meaning word. Write the everyday sense (a guess) and the scientific sense (a well-tested explanation) side by side. Avoid the phrase just a theory. Give examples such as germ theory, cell theory and plate tectonics so students see that theories explain a great deal.
notes.va.paradigm.n: Paradigm is the most abstract word in the unit. Use a concrete picture: the Earth-centered and Sun-centered models of the solar system. Ask what changed besides the model (methods, questions, what counted as evidence). The phrase paradigm shift was popularized by the philosopher Thomas Kuhn.
notes.va.causation.n: Causation is the noun for one thing making another happen. Always pair it with correlation, and use funny pairs such as ice cream sales and sunburns. Note the spelling: cause loses its e before -ation. Ask what an experiment must do to support causation.
notes.va.empirical.adj: Empirical means based on observation or measurement, and its opposite in this unit is theoretical. Students may think empirical means true; it means observed, and observations can still be flawed. Practice turning opinion statements into empirical questions.
notes.va.replicate.v: Replicate is to repeat on purpose to see whether a result holds. Contrast with copy: students may think replication means copying someone's answers. A replication uses the same method, not the same data. Link to writing lab steps clearly.
notes.va.anomaly.n: An anomaly is a data point that does not fit. Students tend to delete anomalies or call them mistakes. Use the Uranus and Neptune story in the passage, and the contrasting case of Mercury's orbit (a long unexplained anomaly later explained by Einstein's general relativity in 1915).
notes.va.quantitative.adj: Quantitative is built on quantity: numbers and amounts. Ask students for quantitative and qualitative questions about the same topic. Pair with units: ten what? Notice the matched pair with qualitative and the one-letter difference in spelling.
notes.va.qualitative.adj: Qualitative is built on quality: descriptions of properties and opinions. Students often treat qualitative as worse; show that it explains why. The two words are easy to swap, so use the quantity and quality memory hook.
notes.va.confound.v: In experiments, to confound is to mix an extra factor in so the cause cannot be sorted out. The everyday sense (to puzzle) is shown as a second sense. Ask students to find the confounding variable in three short experiment descriptions and to propose a control.
notes.va.rigorous.adj: Rigorous praises careful, exact method, and the noun is rigor. It does not mean harsh or difficult. A rigorous lab report is one in which others can follow every step. Contrast with sloppy and with merely complicated.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: “The first trial puts the fertilized plants on the sunny sill. That could confound the results because I cannot tell whether light or fertilizer made them taller. For a rigorous second test I would give every plant the same light and choose groups by chance. One plant wilted. It is an anomaly, so I will not delete it. I will check it, and if I can replicate the setup, I will see whether it happens again.”
discuss: Which is more convincing: one surprising study or five similar studies by different teams? Why?
Can a theory ever be proven completely? What does it mean to say a theory is well supported?
How does a news headline sometimes confuse correlation with causation?
misconceptions: A theory is just a guess that has not been proven yet.
Qualitative data are less scientific than quantitative data.
An anomaly is a mistake and should be thrown out.
extend: Collect three news headlines about scientific studies and decide which claim causation and which only show correlation.
Design a rigorous test of a school-yard question (such as which paper airplane flies farthest), naming the variables you will control.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit hypothesize, extrapolate, postulate and corroborate from grade 7 by asking students to write one sentence per word about the beans experiment. Return to confound and replicate two days later with a new experiment description, and again when the technology unit discusses studies about screens and sleep.

To make the test more rigorous, I would ___.

wida.oral: Partner A describes an experiment with one flaw. Partner B names the flaw with confound or anomaly and suggests how to replicate the test more rigorously.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: teoría, paradigma, causalidad (for causation), empírico, replicar (also means reply in Spanish), cuantitativo, cualitativo, confundir (sense: mix a variable in), riguroso.

Fact claims in the passage and notes to confirm: Uranus's orbit anomaly in the 1840s and the discovery of Neptune in 1846 where calculations pointed; acceptance of the Sun-centered model; plate tectonics, germ theory and cell theory as examples of theories; Mercury's anomaly explained by general relativity in 1915; paradigm shift popularized by Thomas Kuhn.
Sense boundaries: theory (scientific sense taught, everyday sense as a second sense); confound (experimental-design sense taught, puzzle sense as a second sense).
The relation of the headwords quantitative and qualitative to quantity and quality is stated as a memory hook only; no etymology is claimed.
